scope: generic controller literacy, goal setting, interaction design, and game design only; no ARC game-specific knowledge

principles.text: Directional controls such as D-pad, arrow keys, WASD, or left stick are usually candidates for movement or navigation.
Buttons such as A/B/X/Y, face buttons, space, enter, mouse buttons, shoulder buttons, and triggers are usually candidates for primary, secondary, contextual, or mode-changing actions.
Start, Select, Menu, View, Escape, and similar controls are usually candidates for starting, pausing, opening menus, confirming, cancelling, or changing interface state rather than ordinary movement.
Game Boy pattern: D-pad for directions; A/B for primary and secondary actions; Start and Select for game/system functions.
NES pattern: D-pad for directions; A/B for actions; Start and Select for game/system functions.
SNES pattern: D-pad for directions; A/B/X/Y for actions; L/R for additional actions; Start and Select for game/system functions.
Xbox-style pattern: left stick or D-pad for movement/navigation; right stick often for camera/aim; A/B/X/Y for actions; LB/RB and LT/RT for secondary actions; Menu/View for system functions.

PC pattern: WASD or arrows often map to movement; mouse movement often maps to pointing/camera; left/right click, space, enter, shift, control, and number keys are common action candidates; Escape often maps to pause/back.
When the game is unknown, first form a short-term goal to discover what is controllable and which available actions produce meaningful state changes.
Treat changes in position, reachable area, object state, score, counters, inventory, level state, or other persistent environment changes as evidence that an action may advance progress.
Maintain a provisional current goal rather than assuming the final objective. Keep it when observations support progress and revise it when repeated evidence contradicts it.
If the same action in an equivalent state repeatedly produces no useful change, stop prioritizing that action for the current goal and test another plausible control.
When the environment reveals a clear success, completion, score, or progression signal, promote that signal to the primary goal.

Interactive systems expose affordances: spatial placement, shapes, highlighting, boundaries, objects, and controls may indicate possible interactions, but their meaning must be confirmed by observation.
Evaluate an action by comparing the environment immediately before and after it. Visual, spatial, numerical, modal, or object changes are feedback.
When an action has no effect, possible explanations include a boundary, obstacle, unmet precondition, wrong context, inactive control, or already-satisfied state. Do not assume only one explanation.
Unknown controls should be probed systematically. Prefer testing unresolved controls over repeatedly issuing a control whose effect is already known to be unhelpful.
A control that produced a kind of effect before is evidence for a stable role, although context may change its effect. Reuse that evidence when choosing future actions.
Games usually contain an explicit or implicit success condition. Infer it from feedback and progression signals rather than assuming a specific objective such as exit, collection, or combat.
Games are governed by learnable rules connecting state, action, and consequence. Preserve useful observations that reveal those rules.
The controllable entity may have position, mode, inventory, health, capabilities, or other state. A change in these can alter which actions are useful.
Environment elements may be obstacles, targets, resources, switches, hazards, decorations, or mechanisms. Determine their role from interaction evidence rather than appearance alone.
Some objects or counters may be collected, consumed, accumulated, spent, or required as preconditions. Treat persistent count/state changes as evidence of resource mechanics.
Blocked or harmful transitions may indicate obstacles or hazards. Useful responses can include avoiding, navigating around, changing state, or satisfying a precondition.

Score gain, new area, unlocked state, new capability, object acquisition, or level transition can signal progress; reset, lost state, negative score, or blocked progress can signal penalty or failure.
Games often progress through states or levels. Previously learned control roles and interaction rules may remain useful across later states unless evidence changes.
When an unexplained useful transition occurs, retain the before-state, action, after-state, and observed effect as evidence for future decisions.
